newsitem.title: FRANCE: French aid group blasts governments over security.
newsitem.headline: French aid group blasts governments over security.

text.p: Governments and rebels in the world's troublespots are forcing relief workers to take ever more responsibility for protecting civilians, with often tragic results, Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF) said on Thursday.
The annual report of the medical charity, which marks its 25th anniversary this year, urged Western governments especially to stop using it and other similar agencies as smokescreens.

"More than ever, relief work has to tackle the issue of protecting civilians in conflicts where they are not only targets but also used as hostages or human shields," Doris Schopper, president of the international council of MSF (Doctors Without Borders), wrote in "World in Crisis".

But volunteers like the "French doctors" can be powerless to intervene. In Rwanda, 3,000 Hutus were slaughtered in April 1995 by army soldiers at a camp in Kibeho, a massacre witnessed by MSF workers and United Nations peacekeepers.
"As always, those who had the will to protect people did not have the means, those who had the power to do this did not have the will," wrote former MSF head Rony Brauman.
Comparing Kibeho to massacres in the Bosnian enclave of Srebrenica, Brauman said sending U.N. peacekeepers to a hot-spot amounted to the world community doing nothing.

"What is new is that non-state bodies -- Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs), U.N. humanitarian agencies -- are implicitly entrusted the task of protecting civilian populations. That means taking on what is the basic duty of a state -- collective security," Brauman said.
The report highlighted a series of recent crises:

-- When a shaky eight-month truce collapsed in Liberia in April, government forces did nothing to prevent rebels looting relief agencies in a country where "humanitarian aid has been so often stolen that it has been accused of feeding the war";

-- Almost two years after Russian forces intervened in the breakaway republic of Chechnya in December 1994, civilians are deliberately targeted and "relief agencies are prevented from bringing help to civilians trapped by fighting";

-- The war in Bosnia would have ended much earlier if Western leaders had clearly flagged their opposition to "ethnic cleansing" rather than hiding behind humanitarian aid which was put forward as the only possible response;

-- Sudan's war against rebels has caused the death of some 1.4 million people since 1983 and spawned 3.5 million refugees. "If government authorities have allowed relief groups, it is under conditions laid down by the regime's interests."

-- The social and economic crisis hitting France was obviously not as serious as the above, but "in this country at peace, with no massacres or famine...the scale and violence of social exclusion has led humanitarian organisations to intervene."

With branches in 20 nations, MSF traces its roots to the public and media outrage provoked by the horrific images of starving children flashed around the world at the end of the Biafran war in Nigeria in 1970.
It was the first relief organisation to criticise a government openly when it accused the Ethiopian authorities in 1985 of driving a displaced population to starvation.
